doc.title: Claude Williams interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 4, 1995

title: Dancing and jazz today; rock and music education
summary: Dance tempos change but the music doesn't; rock displaced music teaching for years.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: I wanted to ask this, is you know, back then you talk about playing music for dances. How is the jazz different today? Do people still dance to it or has that changed the music?

Well it really hasn’t changed the music but just different styles of dancing with, you know, it need to be different tempos. And so that’ll change the dancing. You know like back in jitterbug days, we’re still playing the same music, but a little faster for jitterbugs you know. And then what made such a big difference in music over here you know, they didn’t teach music in school for about ten years in some schools you know. Along about that time that’s when the Beatles came over with rock & roll and they wasn’t playing that much [scats]. So that’s what they would listen to to dance. They really wasn’t listening to no music, pretty music, or nothing to dance because they just listened to that beat. And that took over for at least ten years. But now they’re teaching music in schools and the kids know what to listen for. When they hear a diminished chord or a minor chord or something, they appreciate that because they know what it is.
